title: Pattern vs Outlier
summary: Pattern = plan for it; Outlier = understand it first — do not base strategy on a single point.

sections.heading: Orientation
sections.subtitle: Lesson Start
sections.contentMarkdown:
- **What will you understand?** **Not** every **strange number** warrants **changing your plan** — you need to know: **Is this a recurring pattern** or an **exception this one time**?
- **Why now?** In the previous lesson, you **extracted summaries** from **AI**. Now you need to **distinguish** what **requires a decision** and what **only needs an explanation**.
- **What after the lesson?** You will classify **5 numbers or days**: **Pattern**, **Exception**, or **Not enough data**.

sections.heading: Tension — One strange number — and you decided to change everything
sections.subtitle: One strange number — and you decided to change everything
sections.contentMarkdown:
- **One day**, sales **tripled** — so I decided to **double the ads**. **The following week**, they returned **to normal**.
- The problem: A **strategic decision** was made based on an **exception**. A **one-time campaign**, a **big client**, or a **recording error** — **not necessarily** a **new system**.
- **Before** acting on **one number** — ask: **Has this happened before?** Or is it the **first time**?

sections.heading: Core idea — Pattern = plan — Exception = understand
sections.subtitle: Pattern = plan — Exception = understand
sections.contentMarkdown:
- Pattern: repeated behavior under comparable conditions can support a provisional plan, checked against a baseline and normal variability; it does not guarantee the future.
- Outlier: an observation far from the usual baseline. Check recording quality and context before interpreting it; it is not defined merely by occurring once or twice.
- Insufficient data: missing context, comparison or suitable periods can prevent a sound conclusion even when you have several points. Collect the needed data or design a small reversible experiment.
- Three observations across three periods are an initial signal to investigate, not a guaranteed reliable pattern. Compare equivalent periods, seasonality and normal variability before generalizing.

sections.heading: Comparison — Reaction to a number versus accurate reading
sections.subtitle: Reaction to a number versus accurate reading
sections.contentMarkdown:
| Decision on one number | Reading before the decision |
|-------------------|------------------|
| Sales on **Friday** **jumped** — **increased ads** immediately. A week later, I discovered it was a **special occasion** | **The same jump** — I reviewed **8 weeks**: **Friday** is always **40% higher**. This is a **pattern** — I **planned** to **increase stock on Thursday** |

sections.heading: Glossary — Two terms to distinguish
sections.subtitle: Two terms to distinguish
sections.contentMarkdown:
| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Pattern** | Repeated behavior under comparable conditions that may support a provisional plan with continued review. | Sales of **cakes** **double every Friday** for **6 months** |
| **Outlier** | An observation far from the usual baseline that needs a data-quality and context check. | **One day** I sold **50,000** and the average is **500** — due to a **wholesale client** |

sections.heading: Quiz — Quick confirmation
sections.subtitle: Quick confirmation
sections.contentMarkdown:
> **Quiz key (unchanged):** correctIndex: 1

**Question:** Your sales **every Friday** are **30-40% higher** than other days — **for 3 months**. **One day only** they **quintupled** due to a **big client**. **What do you do?**

Double the ads** because of the **big client day.
**Plan to increase stock on Thursday** — because **Friday is a recurring pattern**.
Ignore** Friday and the big client — **both** are unimportant.**

**Explanation:** **Friday = pattern** — **worth planning**. **Big client day = exception** — **understand it** but **do not base** your **strategy** on it.

sections.heading: Mission — Classify 5 numbers or days
sections.subtitle: Classify 5 numbers or days
sections.contentMarkdown:
Classify five observations with context, not five isolated numbers. Use your own permitted data or the explicitly fictional sample below. For each value, state the metric/unit, period, comparable baseline and relevant conditions, or declare what is missing. 'Insufficient data' is a valid conclusion. No complex chart, statistical test or real experiment is required.

Fictional teaching case: completed orders per Friday for one shop, with the same opening hours and counting rule. The eight prior comparable Fridays ranged from 90 to 110 orders; this is the supplied baseline, not a forecast. No broader seasonal record is supplied. For the fifth Friday, the fictional order log records 60 orders from one bulk customer within the total. Assess the evidence limits rather than assuming five values prove a future pattern.

| Friday | Completed orders | Comparable baseline | Recorded context |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-04 | 100 | 90–110 | No additional event recorded; seasonal information missing. |
| 2026-09-11 | 102 | 90–110 | No additional event recorded; seasonal information missing. |
| 2026-09-18 | 98 | 90–110 | No additional event recorded; seasonal information missing. |
| 2026-09-25 | 101 | 90–110 | No additional event recorded; seasonal information missing. |
| 2026-10-02 | 160 | 90–110 | One bulk customer accounts for 60 of the 160 orders. |

**Delivery:**

1. Name the metric and unit or denominator, the source, and whether the data are real, fictional or incomplete.
2. For each of five observations: value, day/week and scope, comparable baseline/period and relevant context; explicitly mark missing comparisons.
3. Give a provisional classification for each: pattern, unusual observation or insufficient data, with a reason tied to the comparison and normal variability.
4. Explain whether equivalent periods and seasonality have been checked and what remains unknown; do not treat three occurrences as an automatic reliability rule.
5. Choose one justified next step. A provisional plan may follow suitable evidence; 'insufficient data' with a specific collection plan or small reversible experiment is equally valid. Do not invent a pattern.

| Dimension | Weight | Criteria |
|---|---|---|
| Context and classification | 60% | All five values include metric/unit, period, context and comparison or explicit gaps. Classifications explain comparable periods and variability; isolated values are not automatically patterns. |
| Evidence-based next step | 40% | The next step follows the available evidence and its limits. Accept insufficient data with a collection plan or small reversible experiment; no forced pattern, guaranteed result or real execution. |

sections.heading: Confidence close
sections.contentMarkdown:
- **I understood:** **Not** every **strange number** warrants **changing your plan**. **The pattern** deserves a **decision** — **the exception** deserves an **explanation**.
- **You can:** **Pause** and ask, **"Does this repeat?"** before **any strategic decision**.
- **Next:** **Decision rule** — **one number** can **mislead you**; the decision needs **comparison** and **related numbers**.
